story: Latin trap descends from southern hip hop and trap, influenced by reggaeton, R&B and urbano music. Ozuna dates it to "El Pistolón" in 2007, by Arcángel & De la Ghetto, Yaga & Mackie and Jowell & Randy in Puerto Rico; De la Ghetto says he began around 2005 or 2006. Its reggaeton artists wanted to bring American hip hop and R&B to a Spanish-speaking audience. Around 2014 Alvaro Diaz, Myke Towers and Fuete Billete posted songs on social media, and in 2015 and 2016 Noriel, Anuel AA, Bryant Myers and others put trap songs on SoundCloud. In July 2017 The Fader wrote that Puerto Rican rappers had taken trap's lurching bass lines and jittering 808s. They rapped and sang through autotune, in Spanish or Spanglish, about street life, violence, sex and drugs. Jorge Fonseca's compilation Trap Capos: Season 1 was the first Latin trap LP to top Billboard's Latin Rhythm Albums. In 2018 Cardi B's "I Like It", with Bad Bunny and J Balvin, became the first Latin trap song to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100. In Argentina, Duki, YSY A, Cazzu and others carried it across South America, faster than in Puerto Rico.

disagreements: Start date: our record says 2015; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_trap?action=raw says "it gained popularity after 2007" and gives "cultural_origins  = 2000s–2010s, in [[Puerto Rico]]"; De la Ghetto is quoted as "performing Latin trap since around 2005 or 2006". https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_latino?action=raw gives "Alta desde 2015 en Hispanoamérica y España" as the start of its popularity, which fits 2015 as the date it took off rather than began.

Tempo: our record says a half-time feel around 70 to 80 BPM; the Spanish article says Argentine artists spread it "con un tempo más rápido del que se escuchaba en Puerto Rico", so the tempo marker fits the Puerto Rican sound, not all of it.
notes: Read the Spanish article (es: Trap latino) and used it for two sentences (SoundCloud artists 2015-2016, Argentina). The 'why' sentence (bringing American hip hop and R&B to a Spanish audience) is the article's own statement, uncited there. Ozuna's and De la Ghetto's dates are their own claims, and the story attributes them.
